children.topic: 1. Biliary Jaundice Pathophysiology
Definition and Physical Thresholds
Yellowish discoloration of tissues and body fluids EXCEPT the brain, CSF, tears, saliva, and milk
Sclera and Under Tongue are the first areas where jaundice manifests because of superficial blood vessels
Conjugated (Direct) Bilirubin Alterations
In the Intestinal Lumen: Direct bilirubin cannot reach the bowel due to obstruction, so no stercobilinogen is produced, leading to pale, clay-colored stools
In the Systemic Blood: Conjugated bilirubin backs up into circulation, filtered by the kidneys (water-soluble), and excreted as dark, tea-colored urine
Bile Salts Distortions
Systemic Accumulation (Blood): Causes severe itching (pruritus), bradycardia (vagal stimulation), and frothy urine
Intestinal Deficiency
Impaired absorption of fats and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K) leading to steatorrhea and bleeding tendencies
Loss of gut bacteriostatic barrier leads to increased bacterial fermentation resulting in offensive, bulky, and frothy stools
Impaired intestinal motility leads to constipation
Ductal Structural Effects (Sustained Obstruction)
Biliary duct dilation and stasis leads to formation of thick biliary mud which predisposes to infection, pus production, and secondary stones

The "White Bile" Phenomenon: Sustained high pressure damages hepatocyte secretory function. Bile excretion ceases and the biliary tree fills entirely with clear, mucous secretions produced by its own mucosal lining
2. Biliary Tract Strictures
A. Benign Strictures
Congenital: Biliary atresia (Types I, II, and III)
Traumatic Biliary Stricture (80% of benign cases)
Etiology: Typically follows cholecystectomy or choledocholithotomy
Complete ligation of the CBD
Localized ischemic injury to the duct wall
Blind ligation of a bleeding cystic artery
Failure to identify anatomy at Calot triangle due to dense inflammation
Applying too much traction at the cystic duct, or ignorance of congenital anatomical variations
Clinical Picture: Post-operative presentation with progressive jaundice or persistent biliary fistula
Diagnosis: Abdominal ultrasound to detect ductal dilation, followed by ERCP or PTC to identify exact level of the stricture
Definitive Treatment: Surgical reconstruction via Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy
Inflammatory (Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis)
Multiple, chronic, alternating intra- and extrahepatic biliary strictures and dilations ("pearls on a string" appearance)
80% of cases are strongly associated with Ulcerative Colitis
Presents with progressive jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, and recurrent fevers
Prognosis: Highly precancerous, strongly predisposes to cholangiocarcinoma
Treatment: Patients are ultimately candidates for liver transplantation
B. Malignant Strictures (Cholangiocarcinoma)
Pathology: Over 90% are adenocarcinomas (sclerosing 80%, nodular, or papillary)
Klatskin Tumor: Cholangiocarcinoma arising specifically at the hepatic duct bifurcation (junction of right and left hepatic ducts)
Clinical Picture: Progressive, painless jaundice with systemic symptoms like fever and rigors
Treatment Guidelines
Operable: Resected via Whipple procedure (pancreaticoduodenectomy) if tumor is in the lower part of CBD
Inoperable / Advanced: Palliative management using biliary bypass (cholecystojejunostomy) or endoscopic biliary stenting via ERCP
3. Ascending Cholangitis (Biliary Sepsis)
Pathophysiology: Biliary obstruction + elevated intraluminal pressure + bacterial infection. Stagnation allows bacteria to multiply and ascend retrogradely into hepatic parenchymal circulation
Bacteriology: Most common causative organism: Escherichia coli (E. coli)
Predisposing Risk Factors
Gallstones (most common cause)
Congenital anomalies, immunosuppression, diabetes, hepatic disorders
Prior biliary instrumentation (ERCP, stent insertion, or stone extraction)
Clinical Presentation
Charcot Triad (more than 70% of cases)
1. Fever (with chills/rigors)
2. Severe right hypochondrial pain
3. Jaundice
Reynold Pentad (5-7% of cases)
4. Altered mental status
5. Hypotensive Shock (sepsis)
Indicates suppurative cholangitis / severe disease and carries a very poor prognosis if unrecognized
Diagnostics (Tokyo Guidelines)
Systemic Inflammation: Leukocytosis, fever, or elevated CRP
Cholestasis: Jaundice and hyperbilirubinemia, with AP and GGT elevated out of proportion to AST and ALT
Biliary Dilation: Confirmed on ultrasound or MRCP showing dilated CBD or obstructive etiology
Definitive Management
1. ICU Stabilization: Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation, blood cultures, and broad-spectrum empiric IV antibiotics
2. Emergent Biliary Decompression: Gold standard: ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction (Dormia basket). If ERCP unsuccessful: Percutaneous Transhepatic Drainage (PTC)
3. Preventive Cholecystectomy: Once acute sepsis has completely resolved, elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy to prevent future recurrence
4. Carcinoma of the Gallbladder
Epidemiology: Rare but highly aggressive and lethal hepatobiliary malignancy
Risk Factors
Long-standing gallstone disease (Cholelithiasis): Present in 90% of cases; risk increases with the size of the stone
Presence of a Porcelain Gallbladder (calcified gallbladder wall)
Gallbladder polyps (adenomatous) and chronic typhoid carrier state (Salmonella typhi)
Pathology
90% are adenocarcinomas
Primary Route of Spread: Direct invasion into adjacent segments of the liver bed (very early and common), followed by lymphatic spread to the porta hepatis lymph nodes
Clinical Presentation
Frequently asymptomatic in early stages and discovered incidentally on final pathology after routine cholecystectomy
Can present as acute cholecystitis, progressive jaundice (tumor compressing porta hepatis lymph nodes), or a palpable, hard RUQ mass
Management
Most tumors are advanced and inoperable at presentation
Operable: Treated with radical cholecystectomy, wedge resection of underlying liver tissue, and thorough clearance of the regional lymph nodes
